question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains a grammatical error. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.
I am having trouble / deciding in / a gift for them. / no error
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. deciding in.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct preposition after the verb "decide" when followed by a noun (indicating choice/selection) is "decide on", not "decide in".

• Rule: The phrasal expression "decide on/upon something" means to choose or select something after consideration. Since "a gift" is the object being chosen, the correct form is "deciding on a gift".

• The segment "deciding in" therefore contains the grammatical error — it should read "deciding on".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "a gift for them." is grammatically correct — "for them" correctly indicates the beneficiary of the gift.

• Option 2: "No error" is incorrect because there IS a grammatical error present in the sentence, in the preposition used with "deciding".

• Option 3: "I am having trouble" is grammatically correct — Present Continuous Tense used correctly to describe an ongoing situation.

NOTE

• Other commonly confused prepositions after verbs frequently tested in SSC exams: "decide on/upon", "insist on", "depend on", "rely on", "congratulate on", "agree to/with".

• The idiomatic verb-preposition pair "trouble deciding on" is commonly used when someone finds it hard to make a choice.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A small island
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Islet.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Islet" means a small island. (एक छोटा टापू/द्वीप)
◦ Example: The fishermen built a small hut on the islet in the middle of the lake.

• The word is derived from the Old French "islette", a diminutive of "isle", literally meaning "little island".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Lagoon (लैगून/खारे पानी की झील): A stretch of salt water separated from the sea by a low sandbank or coral reef.

• Option 3: Closet (अलमारी): A small room or cupboard used for storage.

• Option 4: Isthmus (स्थलडमरूमध्य): A narrow strip of land connecting two larger land areas, with water on both sides.

NOTE

• Related geography-vocabulary words often asked in SSC: peninsula (land surrounded by water on three sides), archipelago (a group of islands), strait (a narrow channel of water connecting two seas).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The company sold the newly introduced car to the highest bidder.
option_1: The newly introduced car was sold to the highest bidder by the company.
option_2: The company sold the newly introduced car to the highest bidder.
option_3: The newly introduced car has sold to the highest bidder by the company.
option_4: The newly introduced car sold to the highest bidder by the company.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The newly introduced car was sold to the highest bidder by the company.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The company sold the newly introduced car to the highest bidder" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the newly introduced car" becomes the subject; since it is singular, the auxiliary used is "was"; the verb "sold" (already V2/V3 form, as "sell-sold-sold") is retained as the past participle; and "the company" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: The newly introduced car was sold to the highest bidder by the company.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is simply the original active sentence, not converted to passive voice at all.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "has sold" wrongly uses the Present Perfect auxiliary structure instead of the required Simple Past passive form "was sold".

• Option 4 is incorrect because it omits the auxiliary verb "was" before the past participle "sold" — a passive sentence must always contain a form of "be" + V3.

NOTE

• "Sell" is an irregular verb: sell – sold – sold. Since V2 and V3 are identical, students must be careful to still insert the correct auxiliary (was/were) when forming the passive.

• Common irregular verbs with V2 = V3 often tested in SSC passive-voice questions: buy-bought-bought, bring-brought-brought, catch-caught-caught, teach-taught-taught, sell-sold-sold.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom that can be substituted in the following sentence.
The young boy was born with a silver spoon in his mouth.
option_1: born with a spoon stuck in his mouth
option_3: born with a spoon that was not of gold
option_4: born to not so rich parents
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. born to riches and luxury.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "born with a silver spoon in his mouth" means to be born into a wealthy family, or to be born to riches and luxury. (धनी परिवार में जन्म लेना)
◦ Example: She never had to work hard for money; she was born with a silver spoon in her mouth.

• The expression originates from the old European custom of gifting a silver spoon to a child at christening — a family that could afford silver at birth was considered wealthy, so being "born with" one symbolised inherited wealth.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "born with a spoon stuck in his mouth" is a literal, distorted reading of the idiom and does not convey its actual figurative meaning of inherited wealth.

• Option 3: "born with a spoon that was not of gold" is incorrect and contradicts the idiom, which specifically implies affluence, not its absence.

• Option 4: "born to not so rich parents" is the opposite of the idiom's actual meaning, which denotes wealth, not poverty.

NOTE

• Other idioms related to wealth/status often asked in SSC: "To live from hand to mouth" (to live in poverty), "To feather one's nest" (to grow rich, often dishonestly), "A self-made man" (someone who achieved success through their own effort, without inherited wealth).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank and complete the collocation.
Always be in ______ with your near and dear ones as life is uncertain and fragile.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. touch.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct collocation is "be in touch with", meaning to communicate or stay connected with someone regularly.
◦ Example: Even after moving abroad, she stayed in touch with her old friends.

• Rule — Fixed Collocations: Certain words habitually pair together in English; native usage requires "in touch with", not "in relation with", "in communication with" or "in connection with", even though these alternatives may seem logically similar.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "in relation with" is not standard English usage; the correct collocation is "in relation to" (meaning "regarding"), not "in relation with".

• Option 3: "in communication with" is grammatically possible but is not the standard fixed collocation used for staying connected with close ones; it is more formal/technical (e.g., used for official correspondence).

• Option 4: "in connection with" means "regarding" or "in relation to" a matter, not "to stay in contact with" a person, so it does not fit this context.

NOTE

• Other common collocations with "touch" tested in SSC: "keep in touch", "lose touch with", "get in touch with", "out of touch with".

• Distinguish: "in connection with" (regarding a topic/matter) vs "in touch with" (staying in contact with a person).

question:
Select the correct direct form of the given sentence.
Professor told me that I could not rescue myself from that bait.
option_1: Professor says to me, “You cannot rescue yourself from this bait.”
option_2: Professor said to me, “You have not rescued yourself from this bait.”
option_3: Professor said to us, “You cannot rescue yourself from this bait.”
option_4: Professor said to me, “You cannot rescue yourself from this bait.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Professor said to me, “You cannot rescue yourself from this bait.”

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given indirect sentence "Professor told me that I could not rescue myself from that bait" must be converted back to direct speech by reversing the standard rules of narration.

• Rule — Reporting verb: "told" (+ object) in indirect speech converts to "said to" (+ object) in direct speech, so "told me" becomes "said to me".

• Rule — Pronoun and tense reversal: Since the narration is being reversed, "I" (the speaker as referred to in the indirect report) reverses to "you" in the quoted direct speech, and "myself" correspondingly reverses to "yourself". The modal "could not" reverses to "cannot", and "that bait" reverses to "this bait" (near reference restored inside a direct quotation).

• Applying these rules: Professor said to me, “You cannot rescue yourself from this bait.”

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it uses "says" (present tense), whereas the reporting verb in the indirect sentence, "told", requires the past tense "said" in the direct form.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "have not rescued" wrongly changes the modal "could not" into a Present Perfect negative structure instead of retaining the modal "cannot".

• Option 3 is incorrect because it changes the listener from "me" to "us", which is not supported by the given indirect sentence (only "me" is mentioned, indicating a single listener).

NOTE

• When converting Indirect to Direct speech, always reverse pronouns, tense backshift, and the near/far reference words (this/that, these/those, here/there, now/then) exactly opposite to how they were shifted while converting Direct to Indirect.

• Common modal reversals: can ↔ could, will ↔ would, may ↔ might — when the reporting verb is in the past tense, these are treated as already backshifted in the indirect version and reverse back to their present/base modal forms in the direct quotation.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Fatigue
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Tiredness.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Fatigue" means extreme tiredness or exhaustion, typically resulting from physical or mental exertion. (थकान)
◦ Example: After the long trek, the climbers were overcome with fatigue.

• The word comes from the French "fatigue", derived from Latin "fatigare", meaning "to tire".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Feebleness (कमजोरी): Physical weakness or lack of strength — describes a state of being weak, not necessarily tired from exertion.

• Option 3: Loaf (आवारागर्दी करना): Used as a verb, it means to spend time idly, avoiding work; it is unrelated to tiredness.

• Option 4: Effort (प्रयास): Means physical or mental exertion or a determined attempt — it is close in context but means the cause of fatigue, not tiredness itself.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Fatigue" useful for SSC: exhaustion, weariness, lethargy, lassitude.

• Do not confuse "Fatigue" (tiredness) with "Fatal" (deadly) — a commonly confused word pair in vocabulary sections.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution’.
I am working hard in order to earn a decent living.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No substitution.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "earn a decent living" is already grammatically correct and idiomatically appropriate in the sentence "I am working hard in order to earn a decent living."

• Rule: The verb "earn" correctly collocates with "a living" (as in the fixed expression "earn a living"), and "decent" is the appropriate adjective meaning "reasonably good/respectable" to describe the standard of living.

• Since no grammatical or idiomatic error exists in the original segment, it requires no substitution.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "buying a decent living" is incorrect because "living" (in the sense of livelihood) cannot be "bought" — the correct collocation is "earn a living", not "buy a living".

• Option 2: "earning a better living" incorrectly changes the meaning of the sentence by replacing "decent" (reasonably good) with "better" (comparative), which is not supported by the original sentence.

• Option 3: "purchase a reputed life" is incorrect both grammatically and idiomatically — "purchase a life" is meaningless, and "reputed life" does not collocate naturally; the correct fixed phrase is "a decent living".

NOTE

• Common fixed collocations with "living": earn a living, make a living, eke out a living, standard of living.

• Do not confuse "living" (means of earning money/livelihood) with "life" (existence in general) — they are not interchangeable in such idiomatic contexts.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom that can substitute the italicised words in the given sentence.
The world needs a global leader who can hold out a gesture of peace
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. an olive branch.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to hold out/offer an olive branch" means to make a gesture or offer that shows a person's desire to end a conflict and establish peaceful/friendly relations. (शांति का प्रस्ताव देना)
◦ Example: After years of conflict, the two nations finally decided to hold out an olive branch to each other.

• The idiom originates from ancient Greek tradition, where an olive branch was a symbol of peace and goodwill, later reinforced by the Biblical story of Noah's dove returning with an olive leaf as a sign that the flood had ended.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Mother wit (सहज बुद्धि): Natural intelligence or common sense one is born with, unrelated to peace.

• Option 2: Halcyon days (सुखद दिन): A past period of time that was happy and peaceful/successful; refers to a time, not a peace gesture.

• Option 3: A grass widow (वह स्त्री जिसका पति उससे दूर हो): A woman whose husband is away for an extended period, or who is separated/divorced from her husband; unrelated to peace-making.

NOTE

• Other peace/conflict-related idioms tested in SSC: "To bury the hatchet" (to make peace, end a quarrel), "To pour oil on troubled waters" (to calm a difficult situation), "To break the ice" (to initiate conversation and ease tension).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word leisure from the given sentence:
After my working hours, I use my leisure time to take care of my flower garden, dig my restricted land, sow seeds and water the plants for proper growth and development.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. working.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Leisure" means free time when one is not working, available for rest, recreation or hobbies. (खाली समय/फुर्सत)

• The antonym of "leisure" among the given options is "working", since "working" refers to time spent in employment/labour, which is the direct opposite of free/leisure time. The sentence itself makes this contrast explicit: "After my working hours, I use my leisure time..."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "growth" (वृद्धि): Means the process of increasing in size or developing; unrelated in meaning to "leisure".

• Option 3: "restricted" (प्रतिबंधित): Means limited or controlled; it is an adjective describing the land, not an opposite of "leisure".

• Option 4: "development" (विकास): Means the process of growing or improving; unrelated in meaning to "leisure".

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs with "leisure" tested in SSC: leisure ↔ work/toil/labour/business.

• Synonyms of "leisure" for reference: spare time, recreation, ease, relaxation.

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence.
Rather than being aggressive, you should be accomodative, magnanimous and benevolent in nature.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. accomodative.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "accommodative" (meaning willing to adjust or fit in with others' needs) — it has a double "c" and a double "m", following the base word "accommodate".

• Spelling key: AC + COMMO + DATE + IVE. The word is often misspelt because one of the doubled consonants ("c" or "m") is dropped, as has happened here — the given word "accomodative" is missing one "m".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "magnanimous" is spelt correctly — it means generous or forgiving, especially towards a rival or less powerful person.

• Option 3: "aggressive" is spelt correctly — it means ready or likely to attack or confront.

• Option 4: "benevolent" is spelt correctly — it means kind and generous.

NOTE

• Other words commonly misspelt by dropping a doubled consonant, frequently tested in SSC: accommodate, committee, occurrence, embarrass, recommend — all of which contain double consonants that test-takers often miss.

• Remember: "accommodate" has two sets of double letters — double "c" and double "m" — a favourite SSC spelling trap.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A group of stars having a particular shape
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Constellation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Constellation" means a group of stars forming a recognisable pattern or shape, traditionally named after its apparent form or a mythological figure. (नक्षत्र/तारामंडल)
◦ Example: Orion is one of the most easily recognisable constellations in the night sky.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Planet (ग्रह): A large celestial body that orbits a star, such as the Earth orbiting the Sun; not a group of stars.

• Option 3: Orbit (कक्षा): The curved path followed by a celestial object around another due to gravity; refers to a path, not a group of stars.

• Option 4: Galaxy (आकाशगंगा): A massive system containing billions of stars, gas and dust bound together by gravity — much larger in scale than a constellation and not defined by a "particular shape" of a small group of stars.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes for astronomy often asked in SSC: Zenith (the point directly overhead in the sky), Galaxy (a huge system of stars), Meteor (a shooting star/space rock burning in the atmosphere), Nebula (a cloud of gas and dust in space).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A huge building with a spacious area to house aircrafts.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Hangar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Hangar" means a large building used for housing and maintaining aircraft. (विमान रखने का बड़ा शेड/गोदाम)
◦ Example: The old fighter jets were kept in a hangar at the edge of the airbase.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Airport (हवाई अड्डा): A complex/facility where aircraft take off and land, including runways, terminals etc. — much broader than a single building for housing aircraft.

• Option 2: Hanger: This is a near-homophone of "Hangar" but actually means a device used to hang clothes; it is unrelated to housing aircraft and is a common spelling trap.

• Option 4: House (घर): A general building for human residence; does not specifically refer to a building for aircraft.

NOTE

• Commonly confused word pair in SSC vocabulary: "Hangar" (a building for aircraft) vs "Hanger" (a device for hanging clothes) — same pronunciation, different spelling and meaning.

• Other one-word substitutes for buildings/structures often tested: Aviary (a large cage/building for birds), Granary (a storehouse for grain), Armoury (a place where weapons are stored).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Did Rani call you?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Were you called by Rani?

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Did Rani call you?" is an interrogative sentence in the Simple Past Tense, formed with the auxiliary "did".

• Rule — Passive of Interrogative Sentences (Simple Past, Yes/No question):
◦ Active: Did + Subject + V1 + Object?
◦ Passive: Was/Were + Object + V3 + by + Subject?

• Applying the rule: the object "you" becomes the subject of the passive sentence; the pronoun "you" always takes the auxiliary "were" in the Simple Past; the base verb "call" becomes the past participle "called"; and "Rani" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: Were you called by Rani?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Did you called by Rani?" is incorrect because it wrongly retains the auxiliary "did" together with the past participle "called" in a passive structure, which is grammatically invalid — a passive sentence never uses "did" with a past participle.

• Option 2: "Was you called by Rani?" is incorrect because the pronoun "you" always takes the auxiliary "were", never "was", regardless of number.

• Option 4: "Are you called by Rani?" is incorrect because it wrongly uses the Simple Present Tense auxiliary "are" instead of the required Simple Past Tense auxiliary "were".

NOTE

• Remember: the pronoun "you" always pairs with "were" (never "was") in the Simple Past Tense of "to be", whether referring to one person or many.

• When converting an interrogative sentence to passive voice, the auxiliary (was/were) moves to the very front of the sentence, immediately followed by the object-turned-subject.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
The decision not
P. to include any kind of wealth or
Q. crisis, has proven controversial
R. income tax, which would be the fairer option
S. for solving the social care funding
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. PRSQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed opening phrase "The decision not" must logically connect to an infinitive construction, so it is followed by P ("to include any kind of wealth or"), giving "The decision not to include any kind of wealth or...".

• This "or" signals a choice between two alternatives — "wealth" and the second alternative must be "income tax", found at the start of R ("income tax, which would be the fairer option"), giving "...any kind of wealth or income tax, which would be the fairer option...".

• The phrase "the fairer option" needs a purpose, completed by S ("for solving the social care funding"), giving "...for solving the social care funding...", which naturally combines with Q ("crisis, has proven controversial") to complete the noun phrase "social care funding crisis" and finish the sentence with its main verb "has proven controversial".

• Full sentence: "The decision not to include any kind of wealth or income tax, which would be the fairer option for solving the social care funding crisis, has proven controversial."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: SQPR breaks the sentence into a meaningless, ungrammatical sequence — it fails to properly connect "The decision not" with an infinitive.

• Option 3: RSPQ disrupts the "wealth or income tax" construction that must directly follow "not to include any kind of", producing an incoherent sentence.

• Option 4: QPRS places "crisis, has proven controversial" immediately after "The decision not", which is grammatically and logically incoherent.

NOTE

• In para/sentence-jumble questions, look first for a segment that must directly follow the fixed opening/closing part (here, an infinitive "to include" must follow "The decision not"), then trace logical/grammatical links (like "or" needing two parallel alternatives, or a noun phrase like "funding crisis" that must stay together) to fix the remaining order.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Belief
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Faith.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Belief" means an acceptance that something exists or is true, especially without proof; trust or confidence in someone/something. (विश्वास)
◦ Example: Her belief in her own abilities helped her overcome every obstacle.

• "Faith" carries the closest meaning — a strong trust or confidence in someone or something, making it the most appropriate synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Promise (वादा): A declaration/assurance that one will do something; refers to a commitment, not a belief.

• Option 3: System (प्रणाली): An organised set of ideas or method of working; unrelated in meaning to "belief".

• Option 4: Religion (धर्म): An organised system of worship and beliefs about a divine power; while related, it is narrower and more specific than the general word "belief", which need not be religious in nature.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Belief" useful for SSC: conviction, trust, confidence, opinion, credence.

• Distinguish: "Faith" (trust/belief, can be religious or general) vs "Religion" (a specific organised system of worship) — "Faith" is the broader and closer synonym of "Belief".

question: Select the sentence which does NOT have a spelling error.
option_1: The art and science of designing buildings is called architecchure.
option_2: The art and science of designing buildings is called architecture.
option_3: The art and science of designing buildings is called archtiecture.
option_4: The art and science of designing buildings is called architectrue.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The art and science of designing buildings is called architecture.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "architecture" — the art and science of designing and constructing buildings.

• Spelling key: ARCHI + TECT + URE. The word derives from Greek "arkhitekton" (chief builder): "archi-" (chief) + "tekton" (builder/craftsman).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "architecchure" is incorrect; it wrongly inserts an extra "ch" combination, disrupting the correct sequence "tect".

• Option 3: "archtiecture" is incorrect; the letters "t" and "i" have been transposed — it should be "archi-tect-ure", not "arch-tie-cture".

• Option 4: "architectrue" is incorrect; the letters "u" and "e" at the end have been interchanged — it should end in "-ture", not "-true".

NOTE

• Related words sharing the root "tect" (builder): architect (a person who designs buildings), architectural (adjective form).

• Other commonly misspelt "-ure" ending words tested in SSC: furniture, temperature, literature, signature, structure.

question:
Select the most appropriate collocation to substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
We congratulated him at his new job. He was delighted.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. congratulated him on.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct collocation is "congratulate someone on something", used to express praise or good wishes for an achievement or happy event.
◦ Example: They congratulated her on winning the scholarship.

• Rule — Fixed Preposition: The verb "congratulate" is always followed by the preposition "on" when specifying the reason/occasion for congratulations, never "at", "with" or "along".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "congratulate him up" is not a valid English collocation; "up" cannot follow "congratulate" in this sense.

• Option 3: "congratulate him with" is incorrect; "with" is not the preposition that pairs with "congratulate" to indicate the reason for congratulations.

• Option 4: "congratulate him along" is not a valid English collocation; "along" does not pair with "congratulate" in any standard usage.

NOTE

• Other verb + preposition collocations frequently tested in SSC: rejoice at/over, delighted with/at, pleased with, proud of.

• Remember the fixed pattern: "congratulate + someone + on + achievement/occasion".

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Inherent
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Inborn.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Inherent" means existing as a natural or permanent quality of something/someone; innate, built-in. (जन्मजात/अंतर्निहित)
◦ Example: Kindness was an inherent part of her personality.

• "Inborn" means present from birth, naturally possessed — making it the closest synonym of "Inherent".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Increase (वृद्धि): Means to become or make greater in size, amount or degree; unrelated to "inherent".

• Option 2: Superficial (सतही): Means existing or occurring at or on the surface, not deep or thorough — this is actually closer to the opposite of "inherent" (which suggests something deep-rooted/intrinsic).

• Option 4: Conclusion (निष्कर्ष): Means the end or final part of something, or a judgement reached by reasoning; unrelated to "inherent".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Inherent" useful for SSC: innate, intrinsic, ingrained, natural, essential.

• Antonym to remember: "Inherent" (intrinsic/built-in) is the opposite of "Acquired" (gained through experience) or "Extrinsic" (external).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Both Reeta and Ronika / has won / the dance competition / this year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. has won.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject "Both Reeta and Ronika" is a compound subject joined by "and", and is therefore treated as plural.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: When two subjects are joined by "and" (and are not treated as a single unit), the verb used must be plural. Since the subject here is plural, the correct auxiliary verb is "have", not "has".

• The segment "has won" should therefore be corrected to "have won", giving: "Both Reeta and Ronika have won the dance competition this year."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "the dance competition" is grammatically correct as the object of the verb "won".

• Option 2: "this year." is grammatically correct as an adverbial phrase of time.

• Option 3: "Both Reeta and Ronika" is grammatically correct as a compound subject; the word "Both" itself further confirms plurality is intended, reinforcing that a plural verb is required.

NOTE

• Two singular subjects joined by "and" normally take a plural verb, e.g., "Ram and Shyam are friends."

• Exception: when two subjects joined by "and" refer to a single person/thing or idea, a singular verb is used, e.g., "Bread and butter is my breakfast." / "Slow and steady wins the race."

• The word "Both" always signals a plural reference and reinforces the need for a plural verb.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Climate change, war and displacement, economic considerations, living conditions, family and clan (2)_________, and, more recently, educational possibilities are all reasons for migration. Because there are several reasons for migration, migration patterns are (3)_________. Potential migrants will not only (4)_________ whether or not to migrate, but also where they will go. Individuals with (5) _________ observed and unobserved features will make diverse decisions and self-select into specific areas.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. diverse.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states: **"Because there are several reasons for migration, migration patterns are (3)_________." The word "Because" signals a cause-effect relationship — since there are many different reasons for migration, it logically follows that the resulting migration patterns are varied/different, i.e., "diverse"**.

• "Diverse" means showing a great deal of variety, which correctly reflects the idea that different causes lead to different, varied patterns of migration.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "assorted" means consisting of various types mixed together, typically used for collections of physical items (e.g., assorted chocolates); it does not naturally collocate with "patterns" in this context.

• Option 2: "uniform" means the same/unchanging in all cases — this is the opposite of what the "because" clause logically implies, since multiple different reasons would produce varied, not uniform, patterns.

• Option 4: "constant" means unchanging over time — again, this contradicts the logic of the sentence, since several different reasons for migration would not produce migration patterns that stay constant/unchanging.

NOTE

• When a cloze blank follows a "because"/"since" clause, always check that the chosen word logically follows as an effect of the stated cause.

• Synonyms of "diverse" useful for SSC: varied, assorted, heterogeneous, multifarious — though note "assorted" typically applies to countable, mixed items rather than abstract "patterns".

Because there are several reasons for migration, migration patterns are (3)_________. Potential migrants will not only (4)_________ whether or not to migrate, but also where they will go. Individuals with (5) _________ observed and unobserved features will make diverse decisions and self-select into specific areas.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. determine.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"Potential migrants will not only (4)_________ whether or not to migrate, but also where they will go." The blank requires a verb meaning "to decide/work out" a yes-or-no question — "determine"** fits perfectly, meaning to establish or decide something after consideration.

• The "not only... but also" structure contrasts two related decisions a migrant makes: first, deciding whether to migrate at all (determine whether or not to migrate), and second, deciding the destination (where they will go).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "settle" means to resolve a matter conclusively or to establish residence somewhere; "settle whether or not to migrate" is not idiomatic English — "settle" does not naturally take a "whether" clause in this way.

• Option 3: "certify" means to formally confirm or attest to something as true, typically through an official document; it does not fit the context of a personal decision about migration.

• Option 4: "induce" means to persuade or influence someone to do something, or to bring about a condition; "induce whether or not to migrate" is grammatically and logically incorrect, as "induce" requires an object to be persuaded, not a "whether" clause.

NOTE

• The verb "determine" commonly takes a "whether" or "wh-" clause as its object, e.g., "determine whether it is true", "determine what to do next" — a useful pattern to remember for cloze/vocabulary questions.

• Synonyms of "determine" (in this sense) useful for SSC: decide, resolve, ascertain, establish.

• The logical link is clear: individuals possess varying (i.e., different) features → this leads to them making diverse decisions — the word "diverse" later in the same sentence reinforces that "varying" is the correct sense needed here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 3: "convincing" means capable of persuading someone to believe something; it does not logically describe personal "observed and unobserved features" in this context.

• Option 4: "experiencing" means undergoing or going through something; "individuals with experiencing features" is grammatically incorrect and meaningless.

NOTE

• The passage's logic (varying features → diverse decisions) is a common pattern in SSC cloze passages: look for a later word in the sentence/passage (here, "diverse") that hints at the correct sense of an earlier blank.

• Synonyms of "varying" useful for SSC: differing, diverse, changing, variable.
